summary: A linguist, Ernst Sittig studied at Jena, Berlin, and Halle (PhD 1909–1911 under Friedrich Bechtel). He served as Privatdozent at Berlin (1923), ordinary professor at Königsberg (1926–1929), and Professor of Comparative Linguistics at Tübingen (~1926–1955).

Working in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology, Steinkellner earned his doctorate at the University of Vienna under Erich Frauwallner (~1957–1963). He served as director at Vienna (1973–2006) and directed the Institute for Cultural and Intellectual History of Asia (1998–2006).

Ernst Trumpp specialized in linguistics, Indology, and religious studies, studying at Tübingen under Heinrich Ewald and Rudolf von Roth (PhD ~1848–1854). He worked at East India House, Tübingen, and became a professor at the University of Munich in 1874.

Specializing in Indology, Buddhist, and Iranian/Central Asian studies, Waldschmidt studied under Emil Sieg, Heinrich Lüders, August Hermann Francke, and Otto Franke at Kiel and Berlin. He held posts at Berlin's Ethnological Museum, including custodian and professor in 1934.

Ernst Wilhelm von Brücke was a scholar in linguistics and physiology. After studying at Heidelberg and completing his doctorate in medicine at Berlin (~1838–1842), he held professorships of physiology at Königsberg (1848) and the University of Vienna (1849–1890).

Ernst Windisch, an Indologist and linguist, studied at Leipzig (Dr. phil. 1863–1868) under Curtius, Ritschl, Zarncke, and Brockhaus. He held chairs of comparative linguistics at Leipzig (1869, 1877), Heidelberg (1872), and Strasbourg (1875).

Ernst Zinn was a scholar in linguistics and other fields. He held academic posts at the University of Hamburg (~1946–1951), Saarland University (1951–1956), and the University of Tübingen (~1951–1978).
Ernst Zupitza was a linguist who earned his Ph.D. at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1892–1896). He subsequently served as Privatdozent at the University of Greifswald from 1901 to 1917.

Ernő Hetényi worked in Buddhist studies and Tibetology, studying as a disciple under Anagarika Govinda (~1952–1985). He founded the Magyarországi Buddhista Misszió in 1951 and the Kőrösi Csoma Sándor Buddhológiai Intézet in 1956.

Ervin Baktay was an Indologist and art historian who studied at the Hungarian University of Fine Arts (1909–1910). He was Curator of the Indian Section at the Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts (1946–1958) and lectured at SOAS in 1962.
Erwin Alexis Schwanbeck was an Indologist and historian who studied at the University of Bonn in 1840 and also studied at the University of Greifswald.

Art historian Erwin Panofsky studied at Freiburg, Munich, and Berlin, working under Walter Friedländer. He held appointments at the University of Hamburg (~1921–1933), New York University, Princeton University (~1935–1968), and the Institute for Advanced Study (~1935–1962).

Erwin Rohde was a scholar of classical philology and religious studies who studied at Bonn and Leipzig. He held academic posts at Kiel (~1870–1876), Jena (~1876–1878), Tübingen (~1878–1879), Leipzig (~1886), and Heidelberg (~1886–1898).

A Sinologist and Buddhist scholar, Rousselle studied in Munich, Freiburg, Berlin, and Heidelberg under Krause, Walleser, and von Staël-Holstein. He taught at Peking, Tsinghua, and Frankfurt universities, and directed the Sino-Indian Institute and China-Institut Frankfurt.
Esben Andreasen, a scholar in Buddhist studies, Japanology, and religious studies, studied at the University of Copenhagen and served as a visiting researcher at Otani University in 1992.
Esha Meher is a scholar in Indology and linguistics who is a graduate student and holds a post at Yale University (attested 2026).

A Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar, Nishimura studied at Hanazono and Kyoto universities (PhD ~1970) and under Zenkei Shibayama. He taught at Carleton College and served as director at Hanazono University (2002–2005) and the Institute for Zen Studies.
Esho Kawasaki is a scholar in Buddhist studies who served as director of the Buddhist Cultural Institute (attested 1999) and president of Kyushu Ryukoku Gakkai (attested 2002).
Esho Mikogami worked in Buddhist studies, Indology, and philosophy. He was a professor at Ryukoku University until 2003 and served as president of the Ryukoku Buddhist Society in 1997.

Esho Sasaki is a scholar in Buddhist studies, Indology, and Tibetology. He held posts as associate professor at Ikenobo Junior College (attested 1979) and professor at Kyoto Women's University (attested 1991).
